chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: Bobby Hackett and Brunis
summary: Kmen talks about playing with Hackett, who could never play loud, and the move to the new Nick's.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And Bobby got his trombone player.
Was he playing louder than Hackett or? No. Brunis toned down or what?

No. For Bobby to be heard, Brunis would have had to tone down, because Bobby didn't play louder for the simple reason that he couldn't play louder. I later, but not too much later, played with Bobby myself. Played in his bands, both big and little. Played at the New York World's Fair with him, for example, with a little band. And played in a place on 52nd Street called The Troc, which is not there any longer, across from the second famous door, the more famous famous door, with a big band. And Bobby just never could play loud. He didn't have to look for it. You know, he never was an accomplished trumpet player as a trumpet player. The way I heard is, he was just a guy with a lot of fine ideas for trumpet. Not all of which he always was able to execute. But even his muffs were often pretty. Yeah.
Well he played guitar, you know, and I helped him a lot with getting unusual progressions. But even without that he had a beautiful ear.
